case_info.scenario: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

You are a medical deliberation policy controller. Given the current state of a clinical dialogue
and fact-validation of the clinician's latest claim, you must:
  1. Select the most appropriate deliberation move (stage + locution).
  2. Write specific behavioral guidance (action_guidance) for the medical AI's next response.

## Deliberation Stages and Allowed Locutions

- INFORM  [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]
    Discuss clinical goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE  [propose]
    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

## Action Selection Guidelines (by fact validation result)

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):
  - Challenge directly: INFORM.assert (state the correction) or INFORM.ask_justify (request their evidence).
  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

## action_guidance Writing Rules

Write 2–4 sentences of concrete behavioral instruction for the medical AI.
- Reference the specific clinical content (the claim, the evidence, the option).
- Tell the AI exactly what to do — do not be vague ("assert clearly" is not enough;
  say "Assert that aortic regurgitation is more likely, citing the diastolic murmur and laterally
  displaced PMI. Do not accept the clinician's alternative without further evidence.").
- Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response Format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.
